title: Ransomware hit a US water plant, then spread to the local government behind it
content_md: Cybercrime , Ransomware Ransomware hit a US water plant, then spread to the local government behind it A new, fast-spreading ransomware brand reached the local government’s network. That’s where our MDR team cut it off. November 24, 2026 Hiep Hinh Ransomware hit an East Coast water treatment plant in November, as attacks on water systems pile up across the country. From there, it reached the network of the local government that oversees the plant. The ransomware was Booba, which only appeared this summer and already accounts for 44% of the ransomware compromises our analysts have handled over the last 90 days. Our MDR team locked down 48 machines at once and saved 45 of them. Water systems are a target our team rarely sees, but they’ve become a growing one. In July alone, CISA saw attackers go after more than 100 internet-exposed water and wastewater systems, and Minnesota reported a coordinated attack on more than 30 of its community water systems. Some of those attacks led to boil water notices and forced operators to run systems by hand. There’s no evidence of anything like that here. In this case, Booba had a head start nobody on our side could see. Our analysts see ransomware arriving from machine
